title: Error Boundaries
summary: **Error Boundaries** are React components that catch JavaScript errors thrown anywhere in their child component tree during rendering, lifecycle methods, and constructors — letting you show a fallback UI instead of crashing the whole app.

subtopics.title: getDerivedStateFromError
subtopics.explanation: A static lifecycle method that React calls when a descendant throws during rendering. It receives the error and must return a plain state object (e.g. { hasError: true }) that triggers the boundary to re-render with its fallback. Because it runs during the render phase it must be pure — no side effects, no logging, no network calls go here.

subtopics.title: componentDidCatch
subtopics.explanation: An instance lifecycle method invoked after a descendant throws, receiving the error and an info object containing the component stack. This is where side effects belong: logging to the console, reporting to a service like Sentry, or incrementing metrics. It does not affect what the boundary renders — that is the job of getDerivedStateFromError.

subtopics.title: Fallback UI
subtopics.explanation: Whatever the boundary renders when it is in the error state. A good fallback is more than a bare 'Something went wrong' message — it should be localized to the failed region, match your design system, and ideally offer a recovery action like a retry button. Never render the raw error message or stack trace to end users, since it can leak internal details.

subtopics.title: Boundary granularity and placement
subtopics.explanation: Where you put boundaries determines how tightly failures are contained, because the nearest boundary above a throwing component catches the error. A single global boundary replaces the whole app on any crash, while per-widget and per-route boundaries isolate failures to a small region. The common pattern layers them: per-widget for independently-failing cards, per-route so a page crash stays on that page, and a global catch-all as a last resort.

subtopics.title: What boundaries do NOT catch
subtopics.explanation: Error Boundaries only catch errors thrown during rendering, in lifecycle methods, and in constructors. They do NOT catch errors in event handlers, asynchronous code (setTimeout, promises, async/await), server-side rendering, or errors thrown in the boundary component itself. Those occur outside React's synchronous render phase, so you must handle them yourself with try/catch and surface them via state.

subtopics.title: Class component requirement
subtopics.explanation: A boundary must be a class component because there is currently no hook equivalent for getDerivedStateFromError or componentDidCatch — React has not shipped a function-component API for them. This is a frequent interview gotcha. In practice most teams reach for the react-error-boundary library, which wraps a class internally so you get a clean, declarative API.

subtopics.title: Resetting and retrying a boundary
subtopics.explanation: Once a boundary is in its error state it stays there until you reset it, since the children won't re-render on their own. The simplest reset is changing the boundary's key prop, which remounts it and gives the children a fresh chance to render. The react-error-boundary library formalizes this with a resetKeys prop and a resetErrorBoundary callback passed to the fallback.
subtopics.example:
<ErrorBoundary key={attempt}>
  <Flaky />
</ErrorBoundary>
// bump `attempt` to remount and retry

subtopics.title: react-error-boundary library
subtopics.explanation: The de facto community standard for boundaries in function-component codebases. It provides a declarative <ErrorBoundary> with FallbackComponent, onError, and resetKeys props, plus a useErrorBoundary hook that lets you imperatively trigger a boundary from event handlers or async code — neatly working around the limitation that boundaries can't catch those errors directly.

foundations.overview: An Error Boundary is a special React component that wraps part of your UI and catches errors thrown by its descendants while they render. Instead of the error bubbling up and unmounting the entire React tree (which would leave the user staring at a blank screen), the boundary catches it and renders a fallback UI such as a friendly 'Something went wrong' message.
foundations.formalDefinition: An Error Boundary is a class component that implements `static getDerivedStateFromError(error)` and/or `componentDidCatch(error, info)`. React calls these methods when a descendant throws during rendering, in a lifecycle method, or in a constructor, allowing the boundary to record the error and render alternative UI.
foundations.whyItMatters: Without an Error Boundary, a single uncaught error during rendering tears down the whole React component tree, showing the user a blank page. Boundaries let you contain failures to a region of the UI so the rest of the app keeps working, dramatically improving resilience.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of an Error Boundary like a try/catch block, but for the React rendering process and across a whole subtree. Anything below it that throws while rendering is 'caught' by the nearest boundary above it, which then decides what to show instead.
foundations.browserPerspective: When a component throws during render, React aborts committing that subtree to the DOM. The boundary's getDerivedStateFromError sets new state, React re-renders the boundary with its fallback, and only that fallback is committed to the DOM. The broken subtree's DOM nodes are removed rather than left in a half-rendered state.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Wrapping a dashboard widget so a malformed data response only breaks that widget, wrapping a third-party embed (charts, ads, maps), wrapping each route so a bug on one page doesn't blank the whole app, and wrapping lazy-loaded components.
foundations.businessImpact: A blank white screen is one of the worst user experiences and a direct cause of lost trust and abandoned sessions. Containing errors keeps users in the product and lets you log failures instead of losing them silently.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Boundaries give you a single, declarative place to capture render-time crashes and forward them to error reporting, so you find out about production bugs from your dashboard rather than from angry users.
foundations.performanceImpact: Error Boundaries add negligible runtime cost. The real impact is recovery: instead of remounting the entire app after a crash, you re-render only the small fallback region, which is far cheaper.
commonUseCases: Wrapping individual dashboard widgets or cards
Wrapping each route/page so one page's crash is isolated
Wrapping risky third-party or lazy-loaded components
Providing a global top-level fallback as a last resort

commonMisconceptions.myth: Error Boundaries catch every error in their subtree.
commonMisconceptions.reality: They only catch errors thrown during rendering, in lifecycle methods, and in constructors. They do NOT catch errors in event handlers, asynchronous code (setTimeout, promises), server-side rendering, or errors thrown in the boundary itself.

commonMisconceptions.myth: You can write an Error Boundary as a function component with hooks.
commonMisconceptions.reality: There is no hook equivalent for getDerivedStateFromError or componentDidCatch yet, so a boundary must be a class component (or you use the react-error-boundary library, which provides a class internally).

visualExplorer.title: Where the error is caught
visualExplorer.caption: A child deep in the tree throws during render. Watch the error travel up to the nearest Error Boundary, which swaps the broken subtree for its fallback while the rest of the tree stays intact.

interactiveExamples.title: A minimal Error Boundary
interactiveExamples.explanation: ErrorBoundary is a class component. getDerivedStateFromError flips hasError to true when a child throws, so the next render shows the fallback instead of crashing. Toggle the buggy child to see it in action.
interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: Clicking the button renders a child that throws; the boundary catches it and shows 'Something went wrong.' instead of crashing the app.

interactiveExamples.title: Fallback with a reset/retry
interactiveExamples.explanation: A good boundary lets users recover. Here the fallback shows the error message and a 'Try again' button that resets the boundary's state, giving the child a chance to render successfully again.
interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: The child fails ~70% of the time; when it does, the fallback offers a retry. Changing the boundary's key remounts it so you can try again.

codeLab.title: Build an ErrorBoundary that wraps a throwing component
codeLab.instructions:
Complete the ErrorBoundary class so it catches errors from its children. Implement getDerivedStateFromError to set hasError, implement componentDidCatch to console.log the error, and render a fallback

Something broke

when hasError is true. The component throws on render — your boundary should keep the rest of the page alive.
codeLab.expectedOutput: The heading and the trailing paragraph stay on screen, and the boundary renders 'Something broke' where <Broken /> would have been.
hints: getDerivedStateFromError is a static method that returns the new state object, e.g. return { hasError: true }.
componentDidCatch(error, info) is where you log or report; it does not change what renders.
In render, check this.state.hasError first and return the fallback, otherwise return this.props.children.

debuggingLab.title: The boundary that never catches the click error
debuggingLab.symptom: A button's onClick throws, the app shows an error in the console, but the Error Boundary's fallback never appears.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: Error Boundaries only catch errors thrown during rendering, in lifecycle methods, and in constructors. The error here is thrown inside an event handler (onClick), which runs outside React's render phase, so the boundary never sees it.
commonMistakes: Expecting boundaries to catch errors in event handlers, setTimeout, or promise callbacks.
Forgetting that async errors must be handled with try/catch (and surfaced via state) yourself.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Handle the event-handler error explicitly with try/catch, store it in state, and either render an inline message or set error state that the rest of the UI can react to.

theory.question: What is an Error Boundary and which two methods define one?
theory.directAnswer: An Error Boundary is a class component that catches JavaScript errors thrown by its descendants during rendering, lifecycle methods, and constructors, then renders a fallback UI. It is defined by implementing static getDerivedStateFromError(error) — which returns new state to trigger the fallback — and/or componentDidCatch(error, info) — which is used for side effects like logging or error reporting.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A component that wraps a subtree and acts like a try/catch for the React rendering process.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: An uncaught render error unmounts the entire React tree and shows a blank screen; boundaries let you contain the failure and show something useful instead.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: When a descendant throws during render, React looks for the nearest boundary above it. getDerivedStateFromError lets the boundary update its state synchronously to render the fallback; componentDidCatch runs afterward for logging.

theory.whyImportant: Resilience is a core production concern, and boundaries are React's only built-in mechanism for it, so interviewers use them to test both API knowledge and an understanding of React's render lifecycle.
theory.realWorldExample: Each widget on an analytics dashboard is wrapped in a boundary so a single bad API response only breaks that one card.

nestedTopics.title: getDerivedStateFromError
nestedTopics.explanation: A static method that receives the thrown error and returns the new state object used to render the fallback. It must be pure and cannot perform side effects.

nestedTopics.title: componentDidCatch
nestedTopics.explanation: An instance method that receives the error and an info object with the component stack; used for logging and reporting, not for changing what renders.

nestedTopics.title: Fallback UI
nestedTopics.explanation: Whatever the boundary renders when it is in the error state — ideally a clear message plus a way to recover or retry.

followUps.question: Can you use just one of the two methods?
followUps.answer: Yes. Use getDerivedStateFromError alone if you only need to render a fallback, and add componentDidCatch when you also want to log or report the error.

followUps.question: What happens if the boundary itself throws?
followUps.answer: The error propagates to the next boundary above it; a boundary cannot catch its own errors.

theory.question: Why must an Error Boundary be a class component, and what errors do boundaries NOT catch?
theory.directAnswer: Boundaries must be class components because there is currently no hook equivalent for getDerivedStateFromError or componentDidCatch — React has not shipped a function-component API for these. Boundaries do NOT catch errors in event handlers, asynchronous code (setTimeout, promises, async/await), server-side rendering, or errors thrown inside the boundary component itself.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A constraint of the current React API: the error-catching lifecycle hooks only exist on class components.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: The error handling lifecycle predates Hooks, and the React team has not yet added a hooks-based equivalent, so a class is required (or a library that wraps one).
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: These errors are excluded because they occur outside React's synchronous render/commit phase, where React has no opportunity to intercept the throw and substitute a fallback. You must handle those with your own try/catch and state.

theory.whyImportant: Knowing the boundaries' limitations is exactly what separates someone who has read the docs from someone who has actually shipped resilient React apps.
theory.realWorldExample: A team wondered why a failed fetch never triggered their boundary — because the error was thrown in an async .then callback, they had to catch it and set error state manually.

nestedTopics.title: Event handler errors
nestedTopics.explanation: Thrown outside render, so use try/catch and store the error in state to show feedback.

nestedTopics.title: Async errors
nestedTopics.explanation: Errors in promises, setTimeout, and async functions escape boundaries; handle them where they occur.

nestedTopics.title: SSR errors
nestedTopics.explanation: Boundaries do not catch errors during server-side rendering; the server framework handles those.

followUps.question: Is a function-component boundary ever coming?
followUps.answer: It has been discussed by the React team but is not available yet; in the meantime libraries like react-error-boundary give you an ergonomic wrapper.

followUps.question: How do you 'catch' an async error in a boundary anyway?
followUps.answer: Catch it yourself and re-throw it during render — e.g. store the error in state and throw it in the render path so the boundary sees it.

scenario.question: Your app shows a blank white screen in production whenever one widget receives malformed data. How would you use Error Boundaries to fix this, and where would you place them?
scenario.directAnswer: Wrap each independently-failing region — especially that widget — in its own Error Boundary so a crash is contained to that region instead of unmounting the whole tree. Place boundaries at meaningful granularity: one around each dashboard widget, one around each route, and a top-level catch-all as a last resort. Each boundary renders a localized fallback and reports the error to your monitoring tool.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A placement/granularity decision about how finely to wrap the UI in boundaries.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: A single global boundary would replace the entire app with a fallback on any crash; fine-grained boundaries keep most of the UI working.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The nearest boundary above the throwing component catches the error, so smaller boundaries contain failures more tightly. You trade a bit more wrapping for much better isolation.

scenario.whyImportant: Placement is the practical heart of using boundaries well; interviewers want to see that you balance isolation against over-wrapping.

nestedTopics.title: Granularity
nestedTopics.explanation: Per-widget boundaries isolate failures tightly; per-route boundaries isolate pages; a global boundary is a safety net.

nestedTopics.title: Fallback design
nestedTopics.explanation: Localized fallbacks (a small 'couldn't load this widget' card with retry) beat a full-page error.

followUps.question: How do you avoid repeating boundary code everywhere?
followUps.answer: Make a reusable <ErrorBoundary fallback={...}> component (or use react-error-boundary) and wrap regions declaratively.

followUps.question: How do you reset a boundary after the data is fixed?
followUps.answer: Change the boundary's key (or use resetKeys with react-error-boundary) so it remounts and retries the children.

coding.question: Write a reusable ErrorBoundary component that accepts a `fallback` prop and reports errors via componentDidCatch.
coding.thoughtProcess: I need a class component because the error lifecycle methods only exist on classes. I track an error in state, set it via getDerivedStateFromError, log/report it in componentDidCatch, and render either the provided fallback (supporting a render function for the error message) or the children.
coding.lineByLine: state starts with no error. getDerivedStateFromError stores the thrown error so the next render shows the fallback. componentDidCatch is where you forward the error to a reporting service like Sentry. render returns the fallback (calling it as a function if it is one, so it can use the error) when an error exists, otherwise the children.
coding.timeComplexity: O(1) for catching and rendering the fallback.
coding.spaceComplexity: O(1) — it stores a single error object.

alternativeApproaches.title: react-error-boundary library
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Use the <ErrorBoundary> from react-error-boundary, which adds FallbackComponent, onError, and resetKeys props and a useErrorBoundary hook for triggering boundaries from event handlers — less boilerplate than hand-rolling.

followUps.question: How do you integrate Sentry?
followUps.answer: Call Sentry.captureException(error, { extra: { componentStack: info.componentStack } }) inside componentDidCatch, or use Sentry.ErrorBoundary which wraps this for you.

followUps.question: How would you let the fallback retry?
followUps.answer: Expose a reset method that clears the error state and pass it to the fallback, or change the boundary's key/resetKeys to remount the children.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Layer your boundaries: a global top-level boundary as a last-resort full-page fallback, per-route boundaries so a page crash stays on that page, and per-widget boundaries for independently-failing regions. A single reusable ErrorBoundary component (or react-error-boundary) keeps this declarative.
productionDeepDive.performance: Boundaries are cheap. The win is that recovery re-renders only the small fallback region rather than remounting the whole app. Avoid putting expensive work inside componentDidCatch since it runs on the error path.
productionDeepDive.security: Never render raw error messages or stack traces to end users — they can leak internal details. Show a generic message to users and send the full error and component stack to your private monitoring service.
productionDeepDive.scaling: As the app grows, standardize on one boundary component and a consistent fallback design system so every team isolates failures the same way and every error is reported through the same pipeline.
productionDeepDive.maintainability: Centralize error reporting in componentDidCatch (or onError) so there is one place to wire up Sentry/monitoring. Prefer composing boundaries via a shared component over copy-pasting class definitions.
productionDeepDive.observability: Wire componentDidCatch to an error reporting tool like Sentry, including error.message and info.componentStack, so production render crashes show up in your dashboard with the exact component path that failed.

caseStudies.problem: One widget's malformed API response blanked the entire dashboard.
caseStudies.solution: Wrapped each widget in its own Error Boundary that shows a small retry card and reports to Sentry.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: A little more wrapping and a few extra components vs. failures contained to a single card.
caseStudies.lessons: Fine-grained boundaries around independently-failing regions are the most effective way to keep an app usable when something breaks.

keyTakeaways: An Error Boundary is a class component that catches errors thrown by descendants during rendering, lifecycle, and constructors.
Define it with static getDerivedStateFromError (render the fallback) and/or componentDidCatch (log/report).
Boundaries must be class components — there is no hook equivalent yet.
They do NOT catch errors in event handlers, async code, SSR, or the boundary itself — handle those with try/catch and state.
Place boundaries at sensible granularity (per-widget, per-route, plus a global fallback) and wire componentDidCatch to error reporting like Sentry.
